title: Thames
description:
Archaeological remains associated with the loss of this vessel are not confirmed as present at this location, but may be in the vicinity (see also NPRN 273776 THOMAS).

Event and Historical Information:
The Board of Trade annual statistical report of the shipping losses lists 'THAMES, 40 years, schooner, 91tons, 4 crewmembers, carrying coal' as becoming stranded and a total loss at Penarth Head during the Royal Charter Gale, 25-26 October 1859. 
The Mercantile Navy List of 1858 lists 20 vessels named THAMES- the same vessels are listed again in the 1860 edition. According to Lloyd's Register, the Exeter registered THAMES (official number 11460) was insured as a coaster primarily for voyages to Cardiff. Howver, this schooner had a given tonnage of 95tons and was built in 1826 at Topsham. Crew Lists for the Exeter-registered THAMES continue after 1859.
Contemporary newspaper accounts make reference to the schooner THOMAS, of London, running ashore at Penarth, two men lost'. 
Taken all together, these references suggest that there may have been some confusion in the reporting of the vessel name - the THAMES and the THOMAS actually being. Moreover,the stranded schooner may well have been salvaged and put back into service?

Sources include:
Board of Trade Wreck Return 1859 Table 19 pg25, House of Commons Parliamentary Papers Online document 2623
Cardiff and Merthyr Guardian, Glamorgan, Monmouth, and Brecon Gazette, 29 October 1859, http://welshnewspapers.llgc.org.uk/en/page/view/3091935
Larn and Larn Shipwreck Database 2002

Maritime Officer, RCAHMW, November 2013.

The THAMES was a wooden sailing vessel on passage from Dublin to Bristol in December 1769. The report printed in Lloyds List on 29 December 1769 noted the master's name as Huxtable and that the vessel had been lost in Cardigan Bay with three of the passengers drowned.

title: Thames
description:
This record consists of a documentary reference to a shipping casualty which has been assigned to the maritime named location OFF BARDSEY pending more information which may allow a more precise location for the loss to be assigned.

Event and Historical Information:
The THAMES was a wooden schooner built at Rothehithe in 1819. The schooner was registered at Cardiff on 17 may 1861 (8 in 1861). At that time, the technical and configuration specifications were given as 88.32tons; 58.8ft length x 22ft breadth x 10.4ft depth. 1 deck, 2 masts, square stern, carvel built, timber framework, official number 5329. The owners were George David and Richard Plain, both shipbuilders of Cardiff. The vessel was lost off Bardsey on 20 March 1862. 

Sources include:
Port of Cardiff Shipping Register 1855 - 1865, folio 77, Glamorgan Record Office DRBS1/3

Event and Historical Information:
The THAMES was a wooden schooner built by Marshall at Plymouth in 1875.  Technical and configuration specifications are given as 177gt, 163nt; 103ft 7in length x 24ft breadth x 12ft 7in depth; official number 68346. At time of loss 21 November 1886, the vessel was owned by E F Hickman of London and registered at that port. It was on passage from Port Talbot to Bilbao under the command of master W Morris when it went ashore in Mumbles Road.

title: THAMES TUNNEL
description: The Thames Tunnel, an engineering landmark as the first subaqueous tunnel, was designed and built by Marc Isambard Brunel with the assistance of Isambard Kingdom Brunel as a pedestrian foot tunnel under the Thames. Begun in 1825 and completed in 1843, as well as being the world's first bored tunnel crossing of a river it was also the first example of a shield driven tunnel. Now forming part of the London Underground system, it consists of a rectangulat outer profile with twin side-by-side horseshoe inner tunnels, linked horizontally by brick lined arches; the arches were cut out of the inner wall separating the two bores after the tunnel was completed. The tunnel is constructed from brick using a shield which comprised twelve vertical side-by-side cast iron frames. The twin bores were lined with terracotta tiles which, to afford a uniform profile, were fixed onto 'dentition' brickwork protruding from the structural brick lining. In 1865 it was sold to the East London Railway who converted it to carry their line, opened in 1869, from Wapping to New Cross. Between 1995-1997 the twin bores were relined and refurbished.

description: The 3.75 mile long Thames Haven Railway opened in 1855 from Mucking to Thames Haven. Here connection was made with the Margate steamers. Since 1945 two oil refineries have been located at Thames Haven, raising th line's importance as a mineral railway.

title: Greater Thames Research Framework
description: The Greater Thames Estuary is an area with a rich historic environment resource; above and below ground, and above and below water. In 1999 the Greater Thames Estuary Archaeological Steering Committee (GTEASC) published the first research framework for the area (Williams and Brown 1999) recognising the need for a coherent approach to research in this great European estuary. This document has served to direct research and underpin curatorial decision making for the last ten years. The research framework was not intended to be a static document and a review process has taken place, overseen by GTEASC (with funding from English Heritage). The Greater Thames Historic Environment Research Framework 2010 presents the results of that review.

title: SHAD THAMES
description: "Summary: Remains of the 1918 wreck of an English cargo vessel which foundered approximately 15.5 nautical miles SW of Hartland Point, after colliding with the Norwegian cargo vessel HORTENSE LEA. She was en route from Rouen to Swansea, in ballast. This wreck was formerly thought to be the remains of the TOWNELEY, whose remains have now been positively identified 2.5 nautical miles to the NE (see 1601124)."
